subject: economics
title: Protectionism
welcome_lead: Tariffs, quotas and dumping - when politics blocks trade.
meta_desc: A-Level Trade: tariffs, quotas, subsidies, dumping.
final_note: Protection helps domestic producers but usually harms consumers more.

concepts.def: Selling exports below cost or below home price.
Justification for temporary protection of new industries.

walkthroughs.body_html: A tariff raises import prices, shifting demand to domestic producers. Government earns revenue, consumers pay more, and deadweight loss arises.
A quota caps quantity rather than raising price. Foreign producers (or licence holders) capture the rents that would otherwise go to the government as tariff revenue.
Common arguments include infant industries, strategic sectors, employment and anti-dumping. Each is plausible in theory but is often abused as cover for politically connected industries.

mcqs.q: A tariff is best described as:

options: Selling exports below cost or below home price

mcqs.q: Why do economists generally argue against protectionism?
options: Protectionism means protecting national parks from development.

Tariffs and quotas raise prices for consumers, protect inefficient industries, invite retaliation, and reduce overall welfare — even when they save specific jobs, the cost per job saved typically exceeds the wage.
Comparative advantage means richer countries should help poorer ones.
Protectionism always makes a country richer by keeping money at home.

mcqs.q: What is the principle of comparative advantage?
options: Countries should specialise in producing goods with lower opportunity cost relative to others — even a country worse at everything still has a comparative advantage in something.
A country should produce whatever it can make best.
Comparative advantage means richer countries should help poorer ones.
Protectionism means protecting national parks from development.

mcqs.q: Is a trade deficit necessarily bad?
options: A trade deficit means a country has no factories.
A trade deficit always means a country is losing wealth and failing economically.
Not necessarily — it can reflect strong domestic demand, attractive investment opportunities, or borrowing to fund growth. Context matters more than the headline figure.
